hints: Look carefully at Fig. 9.1 and read off the y-axis value at point A and the value at the far right for the year 2020. What are the starting and finishing concentrations in mg m-3?
Recall the formula for percentage increase as (new value - old value) divided by old value x 100, then round your result to one decimal place.
walkthrough:
Read the Two Values from the Graph**
Point A is the peak at about 330 x 10^3 years before 2020. Read across to the y-axis to get about $540 \text{ mg m}^{-3}$. The line at the year 2020 on the far right rises sharply to about $738 \text{ mg m}^{-3}$. The old or starting value is 540 and the new value is 738.

Apply Percentage Increase and Round**
Use $\text{percentage increase} = \frac{\text{new - old}}{\text{old}} \times 100$. So $\frac{738-540}{540} \times 100 = \frac{198}{540} \times 100 = 36.666...\%$. To one decimal place this is $36.7\%$. Always show working and include the % sign.

hints: Compare the size and speed of the rise after A to all the earlier natural cycles in Fig. 9.1. What does a rapid rise in a greenhouse gas imply for heat retention?
Think about what happens when global temperature rises and ice melts. How could this physically change habitats on land and in the sea?
Consider ocean chemistry as well as temperature. What happens when extra carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater?
Link these physical changes to living organisms. If habitats change faster than species can adapt or migrate, what happens to food chains, biodiversity and extinction risk?
walkthrough:
Link Carbon Dioxide to Warming**
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that absorbs infrared radiation re-radiated from Earth. The very large and rapid increase from about 540 to about 738 mg m-3 strengthens the greenhouse effect, so mean global temperature rises. This is global warming.

From Warming to Physical Environmental Change**
Higher temperatures melt polar ice and glaciers, so sea levels rise, flooding low-lying and coastal habitats. On land there is more drought, forest fires and desertification. In the sea, extra carbon dioxide dissolves to form carbonic acid, causing ocean acidification which harms corals and organisms with shells.

From Environmental Change to Biodiversity Loss**
When habitats change or disappear faster than species can adapt, migrate or evolve, food chains and food webs are disrupted. For example, loss of coral reefs or forests removes food and shelter for many species. Species richness and biodiversity fall and vulnerable species become extinct.

Final answer: Any four: increased greenhouse effect causing global warming / increased temperature; melting ice causing sea level rise and flooding; habitat change e.g. forest fires, drought, ocean acidification; disruption of food chains / webs / ecosystems; change in biodiversity; increased extinction.

walkthrough:
Plants as Resources and Medicines**
Diverse plants provide food, timber for building, fibres for clothing, fuel and other raw materials. Many drugs are first found in wild plants, for example anti-cancer drugs and aspirin-like compounds. Losing species means losing potential future foods, medicines and industrial products.

Genetic Diversity and Ecosystem Stability**
A large gene pool allows selective breeding of crops for disease resistance, drought tolerance and higher yield. In nature, many different producers support complex food webs, maintain nutrient cycling, improve soil stability and reduce desertification. If plant diversity falls, ecosystems become less stable and less resilient to change.

Ethical, Cultural and Economic Value**
Many people believe species have an ethical right to exist and that diverse forests and wildflowers have aesthetic and cultural value. Intact diverse habitats also attract ecotourism, which provides income and jobs while encouraging conservation.

Final answer: Any four: source of resources e.g. food, timber, fibres, fuel; source of medicines / drugs; maintains genetic diversity / gene pool for crop breeding; maintains stability of ecosystems / food webs; prevents soil erosion / desertification; aesthetic / ethical / cultural value; ecotourism income; potential future uses.
